title: Don’t Wait for January: Set Your 2026 Goals Now
author: Chris Martin
source: The Ways of a Gentleman (thewaysofagentleman.substack.com), December 16, 2025
summary: Martin's argument is about timing and architecture: waiting until January to decide who you want to become surrenders the initiative, so the planning work belongs in December. He opens with a borrowed military instrument — the after-action review — reframed for personal use, and supplies four questions, the sharpest being the gap between what you claimed to value and what your calendar actually reflected. The structural core is a three-horizon split (0-90 days, 4-12 months, 1-3+ years) paired with a domain split across physical, athletic, intellectual, spiritual, professional, and relational life, so that ambitions stop being an undifferentiated laundry list. He then imposes a ceiling — seven to ten goals total, one or two per domain — on the argument that anything beyond that becomes noise. A goal is tested by whether it is specific, measurable, realistic given current responsibilities, and requires changed behavior rather than intention, with 'get in better shape' offered as the failing example. The final move is the substitution of systems for willpower: calendar the goal, attach it to an existing habit, track inputs rather than only outcomes, and keep the tracking simple enough to survive. The piece closes on the gap between who you are and who you could become, which it says closes only through decisions made early and reinforced daily.
points: The after-action review is repurposed as a personal instrument, with the best question being the mismatch between stated values and what the calendar actually shows.
The three-horizon split plus a six-domain grid is the piece's real tool: it prevents the undifferentiated ambition list that Martin blames for drift and inaction.
He sets a hard ceiling of seven to ten goals — one or two per domain — arguing that fewer goals with higher standards produce better execution.
The goal test is behavioral, not aspirational: a real goal requires a change in behavior, not just intention, and 'get in better shape' fails it.

Systems are substituted for willpower in concrete terms - calendar the goal, attach it to an existing habit, and track inputs rather than only outcomes, since effort and frequency are what you actually control.
quotes: While most people talk about setting resolutions for the New Year, many often wait until January to set goals, if they do so at all. By waiting the likelihood of moving forward on those goals diminishes. However, by planning now you can evaluate the past year, reflect on your strengths and weaknesses, and solidify your goals so you can hit the ground running in 2026.

Before thinking about your goals for 2026, it is important to conduct, what the military calls, an after action review. This is common after a military operation or training exercise, but can be equally effective for one’s personal life. This is not an exercise in self-criticism, but an honest assessment to reflect on one’s failures and successes in 2025.

One of the most common mistakes people make when setting goals is to make a laundry list of ambitions without regard to time frames. Doing this can lead to inaction and your goals can drift. I like to break my goals up into three groups.

Fewer goals and higher standards will equal better execution. For most people, the optimal number of meaningful goals is 1–2 goals per domain. Progress comes from focused effort applied consistently, not from a long wish list.
Try to avoid complex systems as too much complexity can kill consistency. Track your inputs as much as outcomes. You cannot control results entirely, but you can control your effort and frequency.

If a goal matters to you put it on the calendar and set reminders for yourself. You can also attach it to an existing habit. Doing so reduces the friction to working towards a goal, and it increases the friction of quitting that work.

The gap between who you are and who you are capable of becoming will not close on its own. It closes through deliberate decisions that are made early and reinforced daily through discipline and structure.
